## The checker's report

Check of the Tea Time design sheet (`tea-time`, band 4 to 6), round 1. File read: `games/tea-time/ART.md` as checked, sheet part only (lines 1 to 200).

Records: all ten exist, and code, scope, standing and check state (all `confirmed`) are as the lookup prints today; the summaries are the pack's Summary or the game's own words, with no web address and no suspected paste.
Limits: each "Limits taken" line was compared with that record's Limits; one use goes beyond a record (`us-ca 3.1` at `twins`), and two record links credit the child with tidying that the guests do.
Levels: ages 4, 5 and 6 in both jurisdictions are as printed (us-ca official, nl convention, cross-grade and end-of-primary labels, no gap line); the "no record" sentences hold against the grade 1, kindergarten and preschool lanes; two lane facts are missing (findings 7 and 10).

Findings

1. **The band and its age rule, line 13; the grid, line 33.** The grid has a fifth action, "Rub it", but line 13 lists only tap, hold and drag, and nothing says how a rub differs from a carry, so the third and fifth columns cannot be told apart.
   - Line 13, replace the sentence "Every act is a tap, a press that is held, or a drag that survives a lifted finger." with:
     `Every act is a tap, a press that is held, or a drag: a drag that goes somewhere carries a thing and survives a lifted finger, and a drag to and fro on the spot is a rub.`
   - Line 33, replace the whole line with:
     `Six things, five things a finger can do. A press that is held always means the same: the pot pours onto whatever is under the finger for as long as it stays. To carry a thing is a drag that goes somewhere: the thing leans after the finger and starts to follow once the finger has gone further than the thing is wide. "Put it on" is a carry that ends on another thing; a carry survives a lifted finger. A rub is a drag to and fro on the spot: the finger turns back before it has gone further than the thing is wide, and the thing stays where it stands.`

2. **The grid, lines 38, 40, 41 and 42.** Eight cells name no sound (saucer carry; pot hold and rub; sponge hold, carry and put on; guest carry and put on), and every cell must look and sound different. Replace the four rows with:

Under a cup, the cup hops on. On a guest it is a flat hat that slides off. | It squeaks clean and flashes once. |`

Squeezed over a cup (a tap while it lies on one) it gives its tea back in a trickle. On a guest it wipes the face with a squidge, and the guest scrunches. | It scrubs the cloth on the spot with a squeak and takes up the puddle under it. |`

3. **The designed order, line 101.** "Always free to use" contradicts lines 12, 26 and 72, where the sponge and the bowl come out only when they mean something (the cue-table "Avoid" the sheet calls a hard limit). Replace the line with:
   `**A harder option the child can see and pick.** Every cup is always free to use, and so are the bowl and the sponge once they have come out of the tray, so a child can at any sitting pour from cup to cup, share one cup between two guests or fill the thimble from the Mouse's cup. It looks harder because it is: more tea is moving between more cups. Nothing asks for it.`

4. **The designed order, lines 103, 105, 106, 120 and 126.** The position is judged on each guest's first lift, and a guest lifts within a few hundred milliseconds of every lifted finger (lines 130 and 143). So a pour made in two presses is noted as too little, and a child who creeps up to every ring moves a step back. That contradicts the Attention and Guess answers (lines 63 and 65). At `twins` the first lift also always finds the twin's cup empty.
   - Line 103:
     `**How the position moves.** Each guest is noted once in a sitting, as to taste or not. A guest is noted as not to taste the first time it finds, after a pour, more tea than it likes, or tea in a cup that is the wrong size for it. Finding too little in a cup of the right size is not noted, so a pour made in several presses is never a miss. For a Duckling, more than it likes is more than its twin's cup holds, once the twin's cup holds tea. A guest that drinks without having been noted is noted as to taste. When the sitting ends:`

A thing in the hand is stored where it was picked up.``

8. **The records, us-ca, line 160.** Limits of `us-ca 3.1` names three attributes (length, weight, capacity). At `twins` the cups are the same size and what is compared is the tea in them, which is none of the three and is not marked as beyond the record. Replace the line with:
   ``  Limits taken: capacity is one of the three attributes named, and the game uses that one. Earlier age: awareness, with no procedure asked, so the game only puts cups of different sizes in the child's hands. Later age: two objects, as at `whose-cup`, where two cups differ in how much they hold. No units, numbers or measuring tools. Beyond this record, as the game's own choice: at `twins` the two cups are the same size and what is compared is how much tea is in each, which is not one of the three attributes. Left open by Limits: how the two are compared. Side by side and by tipping one cup into the other are the game's own choice.``

11. **Where the two differ, line 191 (ruling 1).** "Filling to a level" says more than the Dutch records carry. They carry the ideas of full, too much, too little and enough, and filling and pouring as ways of getting to know amounts; they do not carry a pouring skill. "The first six positions … alone" also contradicts the same bullet, where California comes in at the laying of places. Replace the line with:
    ``- **Judging enough.** The Dutch records name the ideas of full, too much, too little and enough (`nl rw/m/3/02/fase1`) and filling, pouring over and emptying as ways of getting to know how much things hold (`nl Inhoud / 2`). The California mathematics records named here are about comparing and ordering only. So the judging of a pour against a ring, at the first six positions, is designed from the Dutch records alone, and the game follows them there. The California records come in at `twins`, `whose-cup` and `three-cups`, and at the laying of places from `lay-a-place` on. Pouring as a skill of the hand has no record in either list, and nothing is claimed for it.``

13. **The claim, line 199 (rulings 1 and 7).** "Pouring to a level is designed from the Dutch records" says more than those records carry. "A place for each thing" does not say which record it rests on, and the claim does not say what is taken from the Dutch records apart from the pour. Replace the line with:
    ``Tea Time is designed from two of California's preschool and transitional kindergarten learning foundations for mathematics (`us-ca 3.1` and `us-ca 3.2`, department-published foundations), two kindergarten mathematics standards adopted by the State Board of Education (`us-ca K.MD.2` and `us-ca K.CC.6`) and one statement of California's voluntary guidance on social and emotional learning (`us-ca 2.H.1`, from the cross-grade lane, in a band tied to no grade); and from five statements of the Dutch curriculum institute's guidance, which is not law: three fase 1 goals (`nl rw/m/3/02/fase1`, `nl rw/m/3/04/fase1`, `nl ojw/ds/1/01/fase1`) and two bullets of the peuter mathematics card (`nl Inhoud / 2`, `nl Hoeveelheden / 3`). All ten records are confirmed. From the California records it takes comparing two cups by how much they hold or have in them, putting three cups in order by how much they hold, pairing a saucer and a spoon with each guest (which `us-ca K.CC.6` names as an example way of comparing two groups), and keeping one's place at the table in order with guidance. From the Dutch records it takes the ideas of full, too much, too little and enough, getting to know amounts by filling and pouring from one cup into another, comparing and ordering cups by how much they hold, pairing one thing with one (a peuter bullet, returned only for a child who has only just turned four) and looking after one's own surroundings. The judging of a pour against a painted ring is designed from the Dutch records only, and no California record is named for it. Pouring as a skill of the hand rests on no record in either list, and nothing is claimed for it. The game says nothing about what a child has reached.``
